The year 1896 was the very best in the business experience of the Sun LIFE 
ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA. The fact that the Dominion was in a condition of 
uncertainty and unrest, owing to the Federal elections, rendered it very difficult to 
s€cure business, but notwithstanding this great impediment, the Company’s record 
for the year shows a large increase over all previous years. The above summary of 
the report for 1896 is well worth reading. It represents a good year’s work and 
denotes prosperity and a healthy growth. 

The total income for the year amounted to $1,886,258, an increase of $358,203.91 
over the previous twelve months. 

A splendid addition has been made to the assets, which now amount to 
$6,388,144.66. The increase for the year is $1,022,374. 13—a remarkable showing indeed. 

The surplus over all liabilities is $345,108.65. The valuation of all policies is how 
made on the Hm. four per cent. basis, instead of four and one-half (as authorized by 
the Government), thus increasing reserve on policies by $1,198,184. 44. 

The death rate was again below the expectation, which goes to prove that the 
management has shown the greatest care in the selection of risks.

ANNUAL REPORT. 


In submitting the Forty-sixth Annual Report, the Board of 
Directors gratefully acknowledge the privilege they have enjoyed 
of helping so many young men in regard to their temporal and 
spiritual affairs. That this beautiful building, standing in the 
centre of our city, has had an open door to every young man who 
has sought improvement and help, during 365 days of the past year, 
is cause for special thanksgiving to God, and the sympathy and 
co-operation of our citizens cause us to realize how large a number 
have at heart the welfare of the young men of this community. 

In attempting to place before you the result of the year’s efforts 
we are impressed anew with the importance and vast possibilities of 
this special work for young men. May we have wisdom and faith toe 
enter in and fully possess this land of such bright promise. 

The two lines of efforts kept in view are (1) the preventive 
and restraining work ; (2) the outstretched hand for the rescue of 
young men who have fallen under the power of temptation. The 
restraining influence which keeps young men steadfast to the right 
during that critical time when habits are forming which determine ~ 
character is, we fear, too little appreciated. While we cannot 
tabulate such results in figures, we know that the effect is to be seen 
in the lives of hundreds of our young men. 

A few facts, taken from Committee Reports, will show the extent 
and variety of the work that has been done. From October to April 
the average daily attendance at the building has been 843. From 
May to October, 360. 

The Membership Record, April 30, 1897, stands at 2,003. 
This shows an increase in the Senior Department of 275, and in the 
Junior Department of 66, results largely due to the Membership 
Contest. 

11,653 young men attended the Bible classes and various religious 
meetings. The Young Men’s Bible class had the largest average 
attendance in its history. During the winter the numbers ranged 
from 97 to I40. 

524 classes for physical exercise were conducted by the Director 
and his assistants. The class enrolment was 565 members, and the 
total class attendance was 13,671. 


9 


405 sessions of evening classes were held, which offered instruction 
in thirteen different branches, with an enrolment of 463 individual 
students. This is an increase of IO7 over the past year. 

The Library has had an average of 315 readers per month who 
drew in all 8,456 volumes. This shows an increase of 39 readers 
and of 1,082 books drawn out. The files of the Reading Room 
contain 128 Periodicals and Magazines, and are very largely used by 
members. 

517 young men were counselled, and of these many were assisted 
regarding employment. 

During July and August the Summer Camp was carried on at Lac 
St. Joseph, near Ste, Agathe, and was attended by 28 junior members 
and 40 senior members. 

The cost of the whole work for the past year has been $13,694.69, 
making an average expenditure per member of $9.80, after making 
adequate allowance for rental. Of this amount the members 
contributed $7,916.23, and the citizens, $5,778.46. 

There have been 492 citizen contributors to the current 
expenses. Of these 54 were new subscribers. This number includes 
banking corporations, firms and citizens. This list should be 
increased by at least one hundred new contributors during the 
coming year, and the Finance Committee should be enlarged in 
order to accomplish this result. 

While experiencing more than usual difficulty in raising the 
amount required for our current expenses this year, the Directors are 
most thankful to be able to report to the members that all accounts 
are paid, and that the year has closed without debt, and this, too, 
without calling upon personal friends for supplementary subscriptions. 

The following letter, received from one of our most practical 
business men the day after he paid a visit to the building, at a time 
when the work was in full progress, shows the impression it 
made upon him :— 

NOVEMBER 5, 1896. 


My DEAR Mr. BupcGe,—I cannot allow my visit to the Y. M. C. A., a few 
evenings ago, to pass without thanking you for your kindness and courtesy in showing 
me through the building. To say I was greatly pleased would be expressing only in 
a very feeble degree my great pleasure at the work I saw going on in your various 
rooms and class rooms. I was thunderstruck and surprised and find it beyond my 
capacity to express my pleasure at the great and useful work that is being accom- 
plished for and by the young men of Moutreal, and I am quite sure the influence 
that this Association must exercise on the minds and hearts of the young men must 
be of immense benefit. 

Wishing you and the Association for which you have worked so hard and 
accomplished so much every prosperity. 

Yours faithfully, 
(Signed) Af. GAUL. 


10 


The prominent position of the building makes it an ever increasing 
resort for strangers and visitors to the city. We regard this a good 
advertisement for the Association and the city. 

Social life in the building has received careful attention, but this 
could be greatly enlarged by the formation of ‘‘ Clubs” amongst the 
young men who have common interests, as illustrated by the Chess, 
Bicycle and Snowshoe Clubs. Let there be added a Camera Club, 
a Shorthand Writers’ Guild, a Junior Alumni Association, a Personal 
Worker’s Society and a Bible Study Club. Social features might 
also be pleasantly and profitably introduced in connection with the 
educational work. The formation of these societies would not only 
add to the social life of the building, but would retain and develop 
the interest of valuable men along these important lines. 

The personal Christian work as carried on in the building by the 
officers and members has been the most important factor in this 
work, and while the results cannot be tabulated, we are glad to 
report that it is coming to be more and more recognized as a centre 
where, at any time of the day or evening, sympathy and counsel 
in reference to matters affecting the Christian life may be obtained. 


THE STAFF.—The personnel of the staff at the building has not 
changed during the year. The men have filled their various positions 
with faithfulness and self-sacrifice, and the present efficiency of the 
Association is largely due to their careful supervision. A most 
important Secretary has been added to the staff, viz., Mr. David 
McConaughy, who is now the representative of this Association 
among the young men of India. One-half of his salary and expenses 
on the field is contributed by a firm in this city, composed of 
interested members of the Association, and the other half is contri- 
buted by the Directors and members. That this advanced step will 
be an increasing blessing to the work and to the workers in this city, 
we are quite confident. Mr. McConaughy is the National. Secretary 
for the Young Men's Christian Associations of India. 


PROPERTY.—The building has been maintained in good condition. 
An enlarged coat room is very much required, and the Shower Baths 
and Gymnasium floor need repairs and renewal. Through the loss 
of tenants there will probably be a shrinkage in revenue from rentals 
amounting to $2,000 for the current year. To provide against this 
heavy loss, an increase in the membership fee has been proposed, 
but the Directors hesitate to recommend this course to the 
Association, as it may exclude some from the use of the privileges, 
and they would urge that as many members as possible advance : 
from a “full” to a ‘‘ sustaining” membership, making their fee $10 
instead of $5. If two hundred members are willing to do this, the 
Finance Committee will be asked to provide the balance. Apprecia- 


11 


tions of the benefits already received and loyalty to the work should 
secure this result. | 

The mortgage indebtedness on the building is $51,000. The 
interest charge on this large sum is a heavy burden upon the current 
work, and prevents progress on new lines. At least, one half of the 
debt should be removed as soon as possible. In a city with 
such wealth and generosity as is possessed in Montreal, this should 
not be difficult to accomplish, and we earnestly hope that some good 
friends of this work may, at this crisis, come forward and render this 
important service. 

Brougsts.—By the will of the late W. B. Hamilton, $1,000 
has been donated to the Association. The $2,000 formerly reported 
from the estate of the Jate Robert Anderson will be paid in October 
next. The Directors desire to make grateful acknowledgment of 
these amounts, 


CoMMITTEE Force.—While there has been an improvement in 
the development of volunteer workers, the Directors feel that the 
Committee organization is not what it might be, or ought to be. 
This is the great educator, not only for the Association, but for the 
Christian and philanthropic work of the city. We should have 
at least three hundred men thus securing definite training. The 
opportunity which this work presents demands it. Let us aim 
at this result in the coming year. For what has been accomplished 
by the cheerful, self-denying work of 177 Committee men, the 
Directors desire to offer their grateful appreciation. This shows an 
increase of thirty-nine men over the previous year. 


Reticious Worxk.—Apart from the regular services, which are 
elsewhere reported, there have been two series of special meetings 
for men, conducted by the Rev. D. M. Cameron, of Liverpool, Eng., 
and Mr. John Currie, Evangelist. These series of special meetings 
should be made an annual feature, and planned for well in advance. 
While the Directors are thankful for the increase in the number 
of young men taking part in the Bible study, yet, as this is the 
foundation of the whole, they would ask for the formation of a Bible 
Study Committee who shall outline a plan of graded courses so as to 
meet the needs of the various classes of young men. 

At the Mobile Convention the International Committee decided to 
place a competent Secretary in the field for the development of Bible 
study in the Associations. Let us prepare at once to take advantage 
of the suggestions of this specialist. There should also be developed 
a strong force of organized personal workers. Let these two 
important matters receive prompt attention. 

In addition to the meetings in the building, services have 
been held regularly in the General and Western Hospitals, and now 


12 ; 


we have a request from the management of the Homceopathic 
Hospital. 

RAILROAD MENn.—At the request of the International Committee, 
New York, your Secretary was given the time necessary to visit 
the divisional points on the line of the Grand Trunk Railway 
and report upon the opportunities for this work amongst their men. 
This was done in July and August last. The report submitted to the 
Railway authorities has been carefully considered with the following 
hopeful results:—The Company has granted an appropriation 
sufficient to organize the work during the next three years at nine 
divisional points, and has also granted an appropriation for the 
annual expenses of the work when organized. This is a bright 
outlook for Canada, and one for which we are entirely indebted 
to the active sympathy and co-operation of the present General 
Manager of the Grand Trunk Railway, Mr. Chas. M. Hays. 

The Association work should keep pace with the development 
of the city, and should have buildings and equipment in some 
measure adequate to the demands that will come upon it in the 
greater city that is to be, whose chief glory should be its young men. 

The demand for branches is already upon the Directors, and 
we trust the day is not far distant when they will be fully provided by 
the generosity of this community. There should be branches at 
Point St. Charles, in the north-east section and at Westmount. 
Property owners having suitable lots in these sections cannot do 
better than to keep this Association benevolently in mind. 


In Memortam.—We have to record the following list of 
subscribers and members whom death has taken from amongst 
our number during the past year. This silent list speaks loudly 
of present opportunity and duty :—

have not space, They will please accept our most hearty thanks.
